chapter.title: Data and messaging
chapter.summary: Partitioning, replication and consistency, and asynchronous messaging: how data and work are spread across many machines.

lessons.title: Sharding and consistent hashing
lessons.summary: Splitting data across machines, why naive hashing breaks when nodes change, and how a consistent hash ring fixes it.

parts.label: HLD
parts.body:
## Why partition

One database server has limits: storage, write throughput, memory. **Replication** copies the same data to many nodes (more read capacity and availability) but every node still holds *everything*. When data or writes outgrow one machine you **partition** (shard): split the data so each node owns a **subset**. Reads *and* writes then scale out.

## Choosing how to split

**Range partitioning**: keys A-F on shard 1, G-M on shard 2... Preserves order, so range queries are efficient. Risk: **hot spots** (all new users have increasing ids and hit the last shard).

**Hash partitioning**: `shard = hash(key) mod N`. Spreads load evenly, but loses key order (range queries touch every shard).

**Directory (lookup) partitioning**: a service maps each key (or tenant) to a shard. Flexible, but the directory is a dependency and a possible bottleneck.

## The shard key is the most important decision

A good shard key has **high cardinality**, **spreads writes evenly**, and keeps the data a query needs **together** (so most queries hit one shard). Bad choices: a timestamp (all writes go to the newest shard), a boolean, a country (a few huge shards). Changing the key later means a painful full resharding.

## The problem with `hash(key) mod N`

With N = 4 shards, `hash(k) mod 4` decides placement. Add a fifth server and the formula becomes `mod 5`: **almost every key maps to a different shard**. Roughly `N/(N+1)` of the data must move, and caches go cold at once. That is catastrophic for a live system.

## Consistent hashing

Imagine the hash space as a **ring** (0 to 2³²-1, wrapping around).

1. Hash each **server** onto the ring.
2. Hash each **key** onto the ring.
3. A key belongs to the **first server clockwise** from its position.

Now adding or removing a server affects only the keys **between it and its predecessor**: on average `1/N` of the data moves, instead of nearly all of it.

### Virtual nodes

With few servers the ring's gaps are uneven, so some servers get much more load. Fix: place each physical server on the ring **many times** (100-200 virtual nodes, hashes of `server#0`, `server#1` ...). Load evens out, and a bigger machine can simply get more virtual nodes (weighting). When a server dies, its load spreads across *many* neighbours instead of dumping on one.

### Replication on the ring

Store each key on the next `R` distinct physical servers clockwise (Dynamo, Cassandra). Reads and writes use quorums (`R + W > N` for strong reads).

## Real systems

- **Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak**: consistent hashing with virtual nodes.
- **Redis Cluster**: 16,384 fixed **hash slots** mapped to nodes (a fixed-slot variant, easier to rebalance in chunks).
- **Memcached clients, CDNs, load balancers**: consistent hashing to keep cache locality.
- **MongoDB, Vitess/MySQL**: range or hash shard keys with chunk migration.

## Problems sharding creates

- **Cross-shard queries and joins** are slow or impossible; denormalise or use a search/analytics store.
- **Cross-shard transactions** need 2PC or sagas.
- **Rebalancing and resharding** moves data online; plan for it from day one.
- **Hot keys / hot shards** (a celebrity user): split the hot key, add a cache, or salt the key.
- **Operational complexity**: monitoring, backups and schema changes multiply by N.

## When *not* to shard

Shard last. First try: indexes, caching, read replicas, a bigger machine, archiving old data. Premature sharding is expensive to undo.

parts.label: LLD
parts.body:
## Design a consistent hash ring

**Requirements**: `addNode(id)`, `removeNode(id)`, `getNode(key)`; virtual nodes; fast lookups; deterministic.

## Data structure

Keep the ring as a **sorted structure of hash positions** mapping to node ids. To find a key's owner, hash the key and find the **first ring position greater than or equal** to it (wrap to the first position if none). That is a **binary search**: `O(log M)` for `M` total virtual nodes.

- Sorted array of positions + a map from position to node (rebuild on change, since changes are rare), or
- A balanced tree map (`TreeMap.ceilingEntry` in Java, `std::map::lower_bound` in C++).

## Classes

- `HashRing { replicas, ring: sorted positions, owners: Map<position, nodeId> }`
- `addNode(id)`: for `i` in `0..replicas`, compute `hash(id + '#' + i)`, insert.
- `removeNode(id)`: remove all its positions.
- `getNode(key)`: `h = hash(key)`; binary search for the first position `>= h`; wrap to index 0 if past the end.

## Choosing the hash

Use a **well-distributed, fast, non-cryptographic hash** (murmur3, xxHash, FNV). Do **not** use a language's built-in string hash if it is not stable across processes (it must give the same answer on every machine and restart). Collisions between virtual node positions are rare but handle them (re-hash with a salt).

## Extension points

- **Weights**: more replicas for bigger nodes.
- **Replication**: `getNodes(key, n)` walks clockwise collecting `n` *distinct physical* nodes.
- **Thread safety**: reads vastly outnumber writes, so use an immutable snapshot swapped atomically (copy-on-write) or a read-write lock.
- **Bounded loads**: cap a node's load and spill to the next (consistent hashing with bounded loads).

## Edge cases

Empty ring (`getNode` returns null or throws), a single node, duplicate `addNode`, a key hashing exactly onto a position (it belongs to that node), and wrap-around past the largest position.

diagrams.title: Lookup: binary search the sorted ring, wrap at the end
diagrams.code:
flowchart TD
  A["hash the key"] --> B["binary search first position >= hash"]
  B --> C{"found?"}
  C -- "yes" --> D["owner of that position"]
  C -- "no, past the end" --> E["wrap to the first position"]

complexity.time: O(V log M) or O(M) to re-sort

complexity.op: Keys moved when a node joins (consistent)
Keys moved when N changes (hash mod N)

keyPoints: Partitioning splits data across nodes so both reads and writes scale; replication alone does not.
Pick a shard key with high cardinality, even write spread and queries that stay on one shard.
hash(key) mod N reshuffles almost all keys when N changes; consistent hashing moves only about 1/N.
Virtual nodes smooth out load, enable weighting and spread a failed node's load across many peers.
Look up the owner with a binary search on the sorted ring and wrap around at the end.

check.q: Why is hash(key) mod N a poor sharding scheme when N changes?
options: Almost every key maps to a different node, forcing massive data movement
check.why: Changing N changes the modulus for nearly all keys, so most data must be re-placed.

check.q: What problem do virtual nodes solve in consistent hashing?
options: Uneven load caused by few nodes landing at uneven ring positions
check.why: Placing each server many times on the ring averages out the gaps, balancing keys across servers.

check.q: Which is a poor shard key for write-heavy data?
check.why: All new writes land on the shard owning the latest timestamp range, creating a hot spot.

lessons.title: Replication and consistency
lessons.summary: Leader and follower replication, replication lag, quorums and the consistency models that follow, with a versioned register in code.

parts.label: HLD
parts.body:
## Why replicate

Keeping copies of data on several nodes gives you **availability** (survive a node or zone failure), **read scaling** (spread reads over copies) and **lower latency** (copies near users). The cost: the copies must be kept in sync, and that is where all the difficulty lives.

## Three replication topologies

**1. Single-leader (primary-replica).** One node accepts **writes**; it streams changes to followers, which serve **reads**. Simple and the default (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB replica sets). If the leader fails, **failover** promotes a follower.

**2. Multi-leader.** Several nodes accept writes (often one per region) and sync with each other. Good for multi-region latency and offline clients; the price is **write conflicts** that must be resolved (last-write-wins, merge, CRDTs).

**3. Leaderless (Dynamo style).** Any replica accepts reads and writes; clients/coordinators send to several replicas and use **quorums**. Highly available; repairs divergence with read repair and anti-entropy.

## Synchronous vs asynchronous

- **Synchronous**: the leader waits for a follower's ack before confirming. No data loss on failover, but writes are slower and a slow follower blocks writes.
- **Asynchronous**: the leader confirms immediately and ships changes later. Fast, but a leader crash can **lose recent writes**, and followers lag.
- **Semi-synchronous**: wait for *one* follower, async for the rest. A common compromise.

## Replication lag and its anomalies

With async replicas, a read from a follower can return old data:

- **Read-your-writes violation**: you post a comment, refresh, and it is gone. Fix: read your own recent writes from the leader, or track a log position/timestamp.
- **Monotonic reads violation**: you see newer data, then older. Fix: pin a user to one replica.
- **Consistent prefix**: effects seen before causes. Fix: causal ordering.

## Quorums

With `N` replicas, write to `W` and read from `R`. If **`R + W > N`**, every read overlaps at least one up-to-date replica. Common: `N=3, W=2, R=2`. Tune: `W=1` for fast writes, `R=1` for fast reads (weaker guarantees). Quorums still allow edge-case staleness (sloppy quorums, concurrent writes), so they are not full linearizability.

## Consistency models (weak to strong)

- **Eventual**: replicas converge if writes stop. Fast and available.
- **Causal**: causally related operations are seen in order.
- **Sequential / Linearizable (strong)**: behaves like a single copy; every read sees the latest write. Costs latency and availability.

## CAP and PACELC

During a **partition** you must choose: stay **consistent** (refuse some requests) or stay **available** (serve possibly stale data). PACELC adds: *even with no partition*, you trade **latency** against **consistency**. Know examples: Cassandra and DynamoDB lean AP (tunable), ZooKeeper/etcd and Spanner lean CP.

## Failover hazards

**Split brain** (two nodes both think they are leader) corrupts data; prevent it with consensus-based election (Raft, Paxos), **fencing tokens** and quorum-based leader leases. Also: promoting a lagging follower loses writes; detection timeouts that are too aggressive cause needless failovers.

## Conflict resolution (multi-leader / leaderless)

**Last-write-wins** (by timestamp; simple, silently drops data and depends on clocks), **vector clocks** (detect concurrency, keep siblings for the app to merge), **CRDTs** (data types that always merge, such as counters and sets).

diagrams.title: Single-leader replication with an async follower
diagrams.code:
flowchart LR
  C1["Client write"] --> L["Leader"]
  L -- "sync ack" --> F1["Follower 1"]
  L -. "async stream" .-> F2["Follower 2 (may lag)"]
  C2["Client read"] --> F1
  C3["Client read"] --> F2

parts.label: LLD
parts.body:
## Design a replicated, versioned register

A small, interview-sized model of leaderless replication: a **key-value store with N replicas**, writes needing `W` acks, reads querying `R` replicas and returning the **newest version**, with **read repair**.

## Entities

- `Versioned<V> { value, version, timestamp }`: every write carries a monotonically increasing version (a Lamport counter, hybrid logical clock or the coordinator's timestamp).
- `Replica`: holds `Map<key, Versioned>`; `put(key, versioned)` keeps the *higher* version; `get(key)`. Can be marked **down** for tests.
- `Coordinator { replicas, N, W, R }`: `write(key, value)` and `read(key)`.

## Algorithms

**write**: create a new version (`max seen + 1`), send to all replicas in parallel, succeed once **`W`** acknowledge, else fail with `QuorumNotReached`.

**read**: query replicas, wait for **`R`** answers, pick the response with the **highest version**. **Read repair**: send that newest value to any replica that returned something older.

With `R + W > N` the read set always includes a replica that saw the latest successful write.

## Design points

- **Merge rule must be deterministic**: higher version wins; break ties by node id, so every replica converges.
- **Idempotent `put`**: re-delivering the same write is harmless (only a higher version overwrites).
- Replicas are an interface (`Replica`) so you can swap an in-memory fake, a network client or a disk-backed store (**Strategy / dependency inversion**).
- Timeouts and retries belong in the coordinator, not in the replica.

## Concurrency and failure

Two coordinators may write the same key concurrently; with plain versions one silently wins (last-write-wins). To detect true conflicts upgrade `version` to a **vector clock** and return siblings. Mention hinted handoff (store writes for a down replica and replay later) and anti-entropy (Merkle trees) as follow-ups.

## Edge cases

Fewer than `W` replicas reachable, fewer than `R` responses, all responses missing the key (return not found), equal versions with different values (tie-break), and replicas rejoining with stale data.

diagrams.title: Quorum write then read with read repair
diagrams.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Coordinator
  participant A as Replica A
  participant B as Replica B
  participant D as Replica C
  C->>A: put(k, v2)
  C->>B: put(k, v2)
  A-->>C: ack
  B-->>C: ack
  Note over C: W=2 reached, write succeeds
  C->>A: get(k)
  C->>D: get(k)
  A-->>C: v2
  D-->>C: v1 (stale)
  C->>D: repair put(k, v2)

complexity.time: O(1) round trips, waits for W acks
O(1) round trips, waits for R replies

keyPoints: Replication buys availability and read scale; the hard part is keeping copies consistent.
Single-leader is simplest; multi-leader and leaderless need conflict resolution.
Async replication is fast but can lose writes on failover and shows stale reads (lag anomalies).
With N replicas, R + W > N guarantees a read overlaps the latest successful write.
During a partition choose consistency or availability (CAP); otherwise trade latency for consistency (PACELC).

check.q: With N = 5 replicas, which setting guarantees reads overlap the latest write?
check.why: R + W must exceed N: 3 + 3 = 6 > 5, so any read set shares a replica with any write set.

check.q: A user posts a comment and immediately refreshes but does not see it. Which anomaly is this?
check.why: The read went to a follower that had not received the write yet.

check.q: What prevents split brain during leader failover?
options: Consensus-based election with quorums and fencing tokens
check.why: A majority quorum can elect only one leader at a time, and fencing tokens make stale leaders' writes be rejected.

lessons.title: Message queues and pub/sub
lessons.summary: Decoupling producers and consumers: queues versus logs, delivery guarantees, retries, and an in-memory pub/sub broker in code.

parts.label: HLD
parts.body:
## Why messaging

If service A calls service B synchronously, A is only as fast and as available as B. A **message broker** sits between them: A **publishes** a message and moves on; B **consumes** it when ready.

Benefits: **decoupling** (they don't need to be up at the same time), **buffering / load levelling** (absorb spikes), **retries and durability**, **fan-out** (one event, many consumers), and **independent scaling**.

Costs: eventual consistency, ordering and duplicate-delivery questions, and one more system to run.

## Two models

**Message queue (point-to-point).** Each message is delivered to **one** consumer among a group, then removed. Use for **task distribution**: sending emails, resizing images, background jobs. Examples: RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS.

**Publish / subscribe.** A message is delivered to **every subscriber** of a topic. Use for **events**: `OrderPlaced` should notify billing, inventory and analytics independently. Examples: SNS, Google Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ fanout exchanges.

**Log-based streaming (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar).** An append-only, partitioned, **retained** log. Consumers track their own **offset** and can **replay**. Each consumer *group* sees every message once, spread over its members; different groups are independent (pub/sub semantics with queue-like scaling).

| | Queue (SQS/RabbitMQ) | Log (Kafka) |
|---|---|---|
| Message after consumption | deleted | retained for days/forever |
| Replay | no | yes |
| Ordering | best effort / per queue | strict **per partition** |
| Throughput | high | very high |
| Per-message routing, priorities, delays | rich | limited |

## Kafka in a paragraph

A **topic** is split into **partitions**; each partition is an ordered log on a broker, replicated for durability. A producer chooses the partition (usually by hashing a **key**, so all events for one entity stay in order). Consumers in a **consumer group** divide the partitions among themselves; one partition is read by one member of a group at a time. Throughput scales by adding partitions and consumers; **ordering is guaranteed only within a partition**.

## Delivery guarantees

- **At-most-once**: send and forget; messages can be lost, never duplicated.
- **At-least-once** (the practical default): retry until acknowledged; messages are never lost but can be **duplicated**.
- **Exactly-once**: only achievable as *effectively-once*: at-least-once delivery plus **idempotent consumers** (dedupe by message id, or make the operation naturally repeatable). Kafka offers transactions within its own ecosystem.

**Design rule: assume duplicates and make handlers idempotent.**

## Reliability patterns

- **Acknowledge after processing**, not before, so a crash redelivers.
- **Retries with exponential backoff and jitter.**
- **Dead-letter queue (DLQ)**: after N failures park the poison message for inspection instead of blocking the queue.
- **Visibility timeout** (SQS): a received message is hidden for a while; if not acked it reappears.
- **Back-pressure**: bounded queues, consumer scaling on queue depth, rate limiting producers.
- **Transactional outbox**: write the business change and the event to the *same* database transaction, and a relay publishes it, so you never lose or invent an event.

## Ordering

Global ordering does not scale. Partition by an entity key to get **per-entity ordering** (all events for `order-42` in one partition). Retries can reorder messages; design consumers to tolerate it (version numbers).

## When to use which

Background jobs and work distribution: a queue. Domain events to several consumers, audit logs, stream processing, event sourcing: a log. Very low latency request/response: do not use a broker, call directly.

diagrams.title: Pub/sub fan-out with consumer groups
diagrams.code:
flowchart LR
  P["Producer: order service"] --> T["Topic: orders (3 partitions)"]
  T --> G1["Group: billing (2 consumers)"]
  T --> G2["Group: inventory (1 consumer)"]
  T --> G3["Group: analytics (4 consumers)"]
  G1 -. "failed 5x" .-> DLQ["Dead-letter queue"]

parts.label: LLD
parts.body:
## Design an in-memory pub/sub broker

**Requirements**: create topics; `publish(topic, message)`; `subscribe(topic, handler)` and `unsubscribe`; every subscriber of a topic receives every message; a slow or failing subscriber must not block the others; optional ordering per subscriber.

## Entities

- `Message { id, topic, payload, timestamp }`
- `Subscriber` (interface): `onMessage(message)`; or a plain callback.
- `Topic { name, subscribers: Set }`
- `Broker`: `Map<topicName, Topic>`; `publish`, `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`.

Pattern: the **Observer** pattern (a topic is the subject; subscribers are observers) with the broker as a mediator.

## Key design decisions

1. **Delivery isolation.** Give each subscriber its **own queue** and worker (or async task). `publish` only enqueues, so a slow subscriber backs up *its* queue, not the publisher or its peers. This is also where **back-pressure** policy lives (bounded queue: block, drop oldest, or reject).
2. **Ordering.** One queue per subscriber processed by a single worker preserves per-subscriber order.
3. **Failure handling.** Catch exceptions from handlers; retry with backoff up to N times, then move to a **dead-letter** list. Never let a handler exception kill the broker.
4. **Thread safety.** Subscriber sets change while publishing: iterate over a snapshot or use a concurrent collection.
5. **At-least-once with acks** (optional extension): keep an in-flight set per subscriber and re-deliver on timeout; handlers must be idempotent.

## Extensions interviewers ask for

- **Wildcard topics** (`orders.*`) with a trie or regex index.
- **Message filtering** by predicate per subscription.
- **Consumer groups** (competing consumers): subscribers in one group share the messages round-robin.
- **Persistence and replay**: append messages to a log and track a per-subscriber offset (this is Kafka in miniature).
- **TTL and retention.**

## Edge cases

Publishing to a topic with no subscribers (drop or retain?), subscribing after messages were published (replay or not?), unsubscribing during delivery, a subscriber that throws, and extremely large payloads.

diagrams.title: Each subscriber has its own queue so a slow one cannot block the rest

keyPoints: A broker decouples producers and consumers, buffers spikes and enables retries and fan-out.
Queues deliver each message to one consumer; pub/sub delivers to all subscribers; logs retain messages and allow replay.
Assume at-least-once delivery and make consumers idempotent; true exactly-once is really effectively-once.
Ack after processing, retry with backoff, and park poison messages in a dead-letter queue.
Ordering is only per partition (or per subscriber queue); partition by an entity key to keep related events in order.

check.q: Which tool lets a new consumer replay historical messages?
options: A work queue that deletes on ack
A retained log such as Kafka
check.why: Logs keep messages for a retention period and consumers track their own offsets, so they can rewind.

check.q: Why must message consumers usually be idempotent?
options: At-least-once delivery can deliver the same message more than once
Idempotency is needed only for pub/sub
check.why: Retries after a timeout or crash redeliver messages, so handling one twice must be harmless.

check.q: In the LLD broker, why does each subscription have its own queue and worker?
options: So one slow or failing subscriber cannot block the publisher or other subscribers
To guarantee global ordering across topics
check.why: Publishing only enqueues, isolating consumers; each worker also preserves that subscriber's order.
